claim: AWS describes on-demand mode as the default and recommended throughput option for most DynamoDB workloads.
question: Which DynamoDB throughput mode does AWS call the default and recommended option for most workloads?

values.display: default and recommended throughput option for most DynamoDB workloads
values.spoken: the default and recommended throughput option for most workloads

qualifiers.scope: DynamoDB tables, choice of throughput mode
qualifiers.condition: most workloads; provisioned mode still fits steady, forecastable traffic

evidence.quote: On-demand mode is the default and recommended throughput option for most DynamoDB workloads.

claim: Effective November 1, 2024, AWS cut DynamoDB on-demand throughput prices by 50 percent and global tables prices by up to 67 percent. Before, on-demand was described as cost effective for spiky workloads; after the cut, most provisioned capacity workloads get a lower price with on-demand mode.
question: What changed in November 2024 for DynamoDB on-demand and global tables prices, and which mode does that favor?

qualifiers.scope: on-demand throughput and global tables, all AWS Regions
qualifiers.condition: global tables cut is up to 67 percent

evidence.quote: Starting today, we have made Amazon DynamoDB even more cost-effective by reducing prices for on-demand throughput by 50% and global tables by up to 67%.
While on-demand was previously cost effective for spiky workloads, with this pricing change, most provisioned capacity workloads on DynamoDB will achieve a lower price with on-demand mode.
These pricing changes are already in effect, in all AWS Regions, starting November 1, 2024 and will be automatically reflected in your AWS bill.

changed.was: on-demand was previously cost effective for spiky workloads

claim: Provisioned mode fits steady workloads with predictable growth, when you can reliably forecast the capacity your application needs.
question: When does AWS say provisioned capacity is the right choice for a DynamoDB table?

qualifiers.condition: capacity requirements can be forecast reliably

evidence.quote: You can choose to use provisioned capacity if you have steady workloads with predictable growth, and if you can reliably forecast capacity requirements for your application.

claim: In provisioned mode you are charged for the hourly read and write capacity you provision, not for how much of it you consume.
question: In provisioned mode, are you billed for provisioned or consumed capacity?

values.display: not how much of that provisioned capacity you actually consumed
values.spoken: you pay for what you provision, not what you consume

qualifiers.scope: per table in provisioned capacity mode

evidence.quote: You'll be charged based on the hourly read and write capacity you have provisioned, not how much of that provisioned capacity you actually consumed.

claim: On-demand mode bills per read or write request, so cost follows actual usage, and a table that receives zero traffic is not charged for any throughput.
question: How is on-demand throughput billed, and what does an idle on-demand table cost for throughput?

values.display: billed per read or write request
values.spoken: billed per read or write request

values.display: you are not charged for any throughput
values.spoken: an idle table pays nothing for throughput

qualifiers.condition: storage and other features are billed separately

evidence.quote: You are billed per read or write request, so your costs directly reflect your actual usage.
If you are driving zero traffic to your table, then with on-demand, you are not charged for any throughput.

claim: On-demand mode lets you create a table without capacity planning, usage monitoring or scaling policies, with pay-per-request pricing so you pay only for what you use.
question: What operational work does DynamoDB on-demand mode remove?

values.display: without worrying about capacity planning, monitoring usage, and configuring scaling policies
values.spoken: no capacity planning, no usage monitoring, no scaling policies

evidence.quote: DynamoDB on-demand enables you to create a table without worrying about capacity planning, monitoring usage, and configuring scaling policies.

claim: The pricing page recommends on-demand mode in most scenarios, including new or existing workloads where you do not want to manage capacity; it names provisioned capacity as the better fit for existing applications with steady, predictable throughput patterns whose capacity you can forecast.
question: When does the DynamoDB pricing page recommend on-demand, and when does it say provisioned may be better?

values.display: On-demand mode is recommended in most scenarios
values.spoken: on-demand is recommended in most scenarios

evidence.quote: On-demand mode is recommended in most scenarios including if you:
Have existing applications with steady and predictable throughput patterns

claim: You can switch a table from provisioned to on-demand mode up to four times in a 24-hour rolling window, and from on-demand back to provisioned at any time.
question: How many times can you switch a DynamoDB table from provisioned to on-demand mode in 24 hours?

values.display: up to four times in a 24-hour rolling window
values.spoken: up to four times in a rolling twenty-four hours

qualifiers.scope: per table, provisioned to on-demand switches
qualifiers.condition: the limit applies to provisioned to on-demand; on-demand to provisioned has no stated limit

evidence.quote: You can switch tables from provisioned capacity mode to on-demand mode up to four times in a 24-hour rolling window. You can switch tables from on-demand mode to provisioned capacity mode at any time.

claim: On August 12, 2025 the limit for switching a table from provisioned to on-demand mode rose from once every 24 hours to four times every 24 hours. Older material and older exam questions may still say once per 24 hours.
question: When did the limit on switching DynamoDB capacity modes change, and from what to what?

qualifiers.scope: per table, provisioned to on-demand switches

evidence.quote: | [Increased limit for switching between capacity modes](#DocumentHistory) | Increased the limit for switching a table from provisioned to on-demand capacity mode from once every 24 hours to four times every 24 hours. This change provides more flexibility for workloads that require loading large volumes of data multiple times per day or need to accommodate unexpected traffic increases. For more information, see [ Considerations when switching capacity modes in DynamoDB](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/bp-switching-capacity-modes.html). | August 12, 2025 |

claim: On an on-demand table you can optionally set a maximum read or write throughput per second, on the table and its global secondary indexes, to keep usage and cost bounded. Requests above the maximum are throttled.
question: What does DynamoDB do when requests exceed the maximum throughput you set on an on-demand table?

values.display: throughput requests that exceed the maximum amount specified will be throttled
values.spoken: requests above the maximum are throttled

qualifiers.scope: per on-demand table and its GSIs, optional setting
qualifiers.condition: applied on a best-effort basis; burst capacity can let some requests through

evidence.quote: When you configure maximum throughput for an on-demand table, throughput requests that exceed the maximum amount specified will be throttled.

claim: The maximum throughput of an on-demand table is applied on a best-effort basis. Treat it as a target, not a guaranteed request ceiling.
question: Is the on-demand maximum throughput setting a hard ceiling on requests?

qualifiers.condition: burst capacity can let requests exceed the setting for a short time

evidence.quote: The maximum throughput for an on-demand table is applied on a best-effort basis and should be thought of as targets instead of guaranteed request ceilings.

claim: On May 1, 2024 the guide added the ability to specify a maximum number of on-demand requests for an individual table, index, or both, to keep table-level usage and cost bounded. Before this, the guide describes no such cap for on-demand tables.
question: When was the maximum throughput setting for on-demand tables added, and what is it for?

values.display: keep your table-level usage and costs bounded
values.spoken: keep table usage and cost bounded

evidence.quote: | [Maximum number of on-demand requests](#DocumentHistory) | You can now specify the maximum number of on-demand requests that an individual table, index, or both, can perform. Specifying the maximum on-demand throughput will help keep your table-level usage and costs bounded and protect against inadvertent surge in consumed resources. For more information, see [Maximum throughput for on-demand tables](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/on-demand-capacity-mode-max-throughput.html). | May 1, 2024 |

claim: Warm throughput is the number of read and write operations a table can instantly support. You can raise it ahead of a planned peak such as a product launch (pre-warming) without changing your throughput settings or billing mode.
question: What is DynamoDB warm throughput and why raise it before a launch event?

values.display: number of read and write operations your DynamoDB table can instantaneously support
values.spoken: the reads and writes your table can support instantly

qualifiers.scope: per table and per global secondary index
qualifiers.condition: works in on-demand and provisioned mode

evidence.quote: Warm throughput refers to the number of read and write operations your DynamoDB table can instantaneously support.
If it’s not, you can increase the warm throughput value without changing your throughput settings or [billing mode](capacity-mode.md).

claim: Once warm throughput is increased it cannot be decreased. Default warm throughput values cost nothing, but you are charged for the requests when you raise them to pre-warm a table.
question: Can warm throughput be lowered after pre-warming, and does pre-warming cost money?

values.display: you will be charged for those requests
values.spoken: you are charged for pre-warming requests

qualifiers.scope: per table or index warm throughput
qualifiers.condition: default warm throughput values are available at no cost

evidence.quote: After warm throughput is increased, the values can't be decreased.
However, if you proactively increase these default warm throughput values to pre-warm the tables, you will be charged for those requests.

claim: A new on-demand table can sustain up to 4,000 writes per second and 12,000 reads per second.
question: How much throughput can a brand-new on-demand DynamoDB table sustain?

qualifiers.condition: warm throughput can be raised ahead of a launch event

evidence.quote: New on-demand tables will be able to sustain up to 4,000 writes per second and 12,000 reads per second.
